crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Drafting Proposals from Past Work
children.blurb: Drafting proposals from past work covers the practice of reusing a researcher's own prior proposals, papers, progress reports and reviewer comments as source material for a new funding application.

children.name: Funder Formatting and Compliance
children.blurb: Funder formatting and compliance covers the rules a funding body places on a proposal before it will be accepted for review, including page limits, font and margin requirements, required sections, reference styles, and the specific templates some agencies mandate.

children.name: Budgets and Allowable Costs
children.blurb: Budgets and allowable costs cover the money a funder agrees to provide for a project and the rules that decide which expenses that money may pay for.

children.name: Finding Collaborators
children.blurb: Finding collaborators for a grant proposal means identifying the people whose skills, data, or facilities fill the gaps in your own team, and whose involvement strengthens the case you will make to a funder.

children.name: Predicting Proposal Success
children.blurb: Predicting proposal success is the use of statistical and machine learning models to estimate how likely a grant application is to be funded, or how it will score in review, before or alongside the actual review.

sections.body: Grant writing in artificial intelligence research is the work of turning a research idea into a document a funding agency will pay for. In practice, AI is being used to mine a researcher's own past papers and prior awards to assemble the background, preliminary results and methods sections of a new proposal. Language models draft and tighten narrative text, check a draft against a funder's formatting rules, and flag missing sections before submission. Retrieval over a publication library helps an author cite the right prior work rather than the most recent or most cited one. Budget tools classify cost lines against an agency's allowable and unallowable categories. Matchmaking tools suggest potential collaborators from coauthorship and topic overlap.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Drafting assistance is genuinely useful and widely used, but it is assistive rather than autonomous. Formatting and compliance checking is the most solved part, because funder rules are written down and can be encoded, though rules change and tools lag behind them. Budget classification works for common categories and struggles with institutional quirks, cost sharing and indirect rate agreements. Collaborator finding produces plausible names but cannot judge whether a person is available, willing or good to work with. Predicting proposal success is the weakest area: funding decisions depend on panel composition, fit with a program's current priorities and review dynamics that are not in any dataset, so any score should be read as a rough signal, not a forecast. None of this replaces the researcher's judgement about what is worth proposing.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages run roughly in the order a proposal comes together. Drafting Proposals from Past Work is the starting point, covering how existing papers and prior submissions can be reused to build a first draft. Funder Formatting and Compliance then takes that draft and checks it against a specific agency's rules on length, structure and required sections. Budgets and Allowable Costs handles the money side, sorting proposed spending into categories a funder will accept. Finding Collaborators steps back from the document to the team, covering how coauthors and expertise are matched to a project. Predicting Proposal Success sits at the end and is the most speculative, describing attempts to estimate odds from past outcomes and text. A reader who wants to write should start at the first page, a reader preparing to submit should go to the second and third, and a reader weighing whether to apply at all should read the last.
